outline.description: Sets out the parties, the marks and services at issue, how the dispute arose, and how it reached the Federal Circuit.
subtopics: Parties and marks: CC Serve’s ASPIRE (credit card services) vs. Apex Bank’s proposed ASPIRE BANK word and design marks (banking and financing services)
CC Serve’s 1998 registration and 1996 priority; CC Serve’s business model of partnering with issuing banks
Apex Bank’s Tennessee retail banking operations; intent to use ASPIRE BANK for an internet bank; Apex does not offer credit cards
USPTO prosecution: letter of protest by CC Serve; publication of Apex’s applications
TTAB opposition under Lanham Act § 2(d) and decision sustaining opposition based on likelihood of confusion
Appeal to the Federal Circuit and scope of appellate jurisdiction

outline.chapter_title: Governing Law and Standards of Review
outline.description: Explains the Lanham Act § 2(d) likelihood-of-confusion framework, the DuPont factors, and the Federal Circuit’s standards of review for TTAB decisions.
subtopics: Lanham Act § 2(d): refusal/oppose registration where concurrent use is likely to cause confusion
The DuPont factors: multi-factor, fact-intensive inquiry; only relevant factors need be considered
First factor: similarity of the marks in appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression
Second factor: similarity/relatedness of the goods/services and marketing circumstances
Sixth factor: number and nature of similar marks in use on similar goods/services (commercial strength/weakness)
Appellate standards: legal conclusions de novo; factual findings reviewed for substantial evidence

outline.chapter_title: Affirmed: The Second DuPont Factor (Relatedness of Services)
outline.description: Details why the Federal Circuit upheld the Board’s finding that the parties’ services are highly similar, supporting likelihood of confusion.
subtopics: Board’s interpretation of “credit card services” in light of deleted ID Manual entry; scope includes issuing, managing, processing, and related account services
Dictionary evidence for “bank,” “banking,” and “finance,” showing overlap with extending credit via credit cards
Finding of legal identity in part: credit card issuance/management fits within banking/financing services
Third-party registrations covering both credit card and broader banking/financing services as evidence of common source
Apex’s counterarguments (non-competition; CC Serve as program manager, not a bank) and why they fail
Federal Circuit holding: substantial evidence supports high similarity; second factor weighs heavily for CC Serve

outline.chapter_title: Vacated: The Sixth DuPont Factor (Third-Party Use) and Its Ripple Effect on the First Factor
outline.description: Explains the error in the Board’s narrowing of comparable third-party uses to only credit card services, and why this requires revisiting the mark-similarity analysis.
subtopics: Proper scope of sixth factor: considers similar, not identical, goods/services; crowded field evidence informs commercial strength
Board’s error: limiting relevant public and third-party marks to credit card services despite earlier finding that services are highly similar/partly legally identical
Federal Circuit’s directive: maintain consistent scope of similarity across factors; include banking and financing services when assessing third-party uses
Consequences for commercial strength: broader third-party use could show conceptual/commercial weakness, narrowing ASPIRE’s protection
Tie to the first factor: commercial impression depends partly on strength; vacatur of first factor because sixth-factor reconsideration may change overall impression
Remand instructions: reassess sixth factor with properly defined scope; then reassess first factor’s appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression in light of any revised strength finding

outline.description: Summarizes the court’s judgment and distills practical lessons for likelihood-of-confusion analyses before the TTAB and on appeal.
subtopics: Judgment: affirmed-in-part (second factor), vacated-in-part (sixth and first factors), and remanded; costs to appellant
Consistency principle: once services are deemed highly similar for one factor, maintain that scope when evaluating other factors (e.g., third-party use)
Third-party use evidence: not limited to identical goods/services; similar goods/services suffice to test marketplace crowding and mark strength
Interdependence of factors: commercial strength (sixth factor) can materially affect commercial impression (first factor) and overall confusion analysis

Practice pointers: build a robust record of third-party uses across the full range of similar services; define service scopes coherently across factors; use dictionaries and third-party registrations judiciously
